The questioner asked, "What?
The Master said,
"The meaning of the coming from the West."
The Master then struck him.
At this, the monk attained great enlightenment.
The Master consequently said:
This old monk observes that the teachers and monks of the present day are all devoid of nostrils,
yet they boast of fame and hanker after profit.
Never resting, he exhorted his brothers: "Each and every thing is *tathatā*;
each and every thing is profoundly mysterious."
If it were not thus, none would escape the conditions of birth and death.
Now tell me: how is it?
"How is it? What is the single phrase that transcends birth and death?
After a long silence, he said:
A single mirror penetrates the bones, reaching every person's intent;
throughout the three periods of time, it is difficult to fathom—each and every one is true.
The Master’s name was Ru Jing.
He was a native of Weijiang in Mingzhou.
His secular surname was Yu, and he was the son of [Yu] Zhen.
He upheld the handle of the Dharma at the foot of Taibai Peak.
The esoteric and exoteric teachings manifest amidst flowing water and incense;
a white heron stands in the snow upon a bright moonlit courtyard.
Green mountains rise straight up beyond the reeds.
Thus, the essentials of the Cao-Dong school once again inherit the original tradition of Dayang;
the blue hawk soars through the nine heavens.
The aged crane perches upon the wutong tree;
those of the time all look up to his profound style.
Relying on him, they engage in question-and-answer sessions and receive his proclamations.
He established the school's style for a generation;
having received the dharma robe from his former master, Fuyong,
he kept it hidden within his quarters.
He took up Old Man Zhuxi’s bamboo staff and leaned it against the wall in the room;
as for the rest of his family instructions and secret teachings—
There is not one [of these] that is not fully understood.
Those who behold this collection shall witness, in a single moment, countless supreme fruits.
This was written in the spring of the Renji *xinchou* year in Japan.

Epilogue to the Continued Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Rutong Ru Jing, written at the residence of Shi Dao-guan of Shu Daochang, dedicated to the guidance and benefit of Xingsheng Baolin Temple. [End of Record]. By the Venerable Rutong Jing. The Venerable Rutong Jing.
The tradition of his lineage is lofty and ancient, peerless in his time;
he transcends both the mundane and the sagely.
Severing all ties to the ten directions:
at times, white waves surge to the heavens atop a solitary peak;
at other times, one sports with supernatural powers amidst the chaos of war.
How appropriate! When the High Ancestor Yongping entered the Song,
a monk named Juejin said:
The one who was a guide for humans and devas and a patriarchal master of a single generation was Master Jing of Chang’ung;
he is the person regarding whom the monastic histories compiled since the Yuan dynasty have recorded.
The details regarding his Dharma heirs are not clear;
however, this present continuation of the records was compiled by the Venerable Waiyi Yuan.
The postscript composed by Yongping Gaozu provides a brief account of these records;
it is as if seeing the bright sun through the rain.
Five hundred years hence,
this record shall circulate in the world;
it is what the High Ancestor meant when he said that it would remain for humans and devas to illuminate the night.
But who, indeed, is the one who knows its worth and its price? Ehi!

On an auspicious day in the second month of spring in the year of Yimui (1595) during the Zhengde era, Haeyun of Sinmun composed this at the heart of Baesujeol-sa on Eagle Peak to the north of Nak, after burning incense and performing nine prostrations.
